items.title: Legal Regulation of Content Moderation in Social Networks: Balance of Public and Private Interests under the Algorithmic Management
items.abstract: Objective: to study current technological and legal concepts in order to determine the legal nature of content moderation in social networks, choose appropriate means of its regulatory regulation, and establish the boundaries of government interference in the activities of digital platforms. Methods: the methodological basis of the work was a set of general scientific methods of cognition (analysis, synthesis, induction and deduction) in combination with special legal methods, including formallegal and comparative-legal. The use of the comparative-legal method made it possible to compare the regulatory models of Russia, China, the European Union, and the United States. The interdisciplinary approach allowed evaluating algorithmic filtering and commercial moderation from the standpoint of public-law and civilistic doctrines. Results: it is proved that moderation of user content is an element of corporate governance of a social network and an integral part of its business model. It was established that, in legal terms, this activity is implemented in three aspects: as a public-law instrument for suppressing the dissemination of illegal content in the interests of state and public safety; as a constitutional-legal guarantee of freedom of speech and fundamental rights of citizens; as a private-law mechanism for protecting the property and personal non-property rights of users and online communities. It is proved that, under hybrid information filtering with artificial intelligence algorithms, the legitimacy of platform control is achieved by a combination of legislative regulation, corporate selfregulation and, user self-censorship. Scientific novelty: the study formulates the concept of balancing the publiclaw goals of suppressing illegal information and protecting the private interests of digital content creators while limiting the discretionary powers of platform owners. The applicability of a private-law approach to content moderation relations is substantiated, including when transferring the functions of checking and blocking materials to external contractors on outsourcing terms, where a third party is actually given public-law powers without direct contractual relations with the user. The article substantiates considering artificial intelligence in the moderation circuit as an element of a sociotechnical system that affects public trust and reliability of the information environment. Practical significance: this is due to the presence of gaps in legislation regarding the regulation of platform moderation procedures, as well as the lack of regulatory certainty of the user’s right to receive an explanation of the reasons for restricting access to content and the right to challenge the decisions of algorithmic systems or moderators. The formulated conclusions can be used by the legislator and operators of digital platforms in improving the legal mechanisms of transparency, accountability and proportionality of content moderation in social networks.

items.title: Liquid biopsy in breast cancer: multi-analyte biomarkers, artificial intelligence, and precision oncology from early detection to therapeutic intervention
items.abstract: Breast cancer (BC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, driven largely by tumor heterogeneity, clonal evolution, and therapeutic resistance. Tissue biopsy, while the diagnostic gold standard, offers only a static snapshot of a constantly evolving disease, and repeated sampling is often impractical, particularly in metastatic settings. Liquid biopsy has emerged as a minimally invasive alternative capable of capturing this evolving biology in real time through circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), circulating tumor cells (CTCs), and extracellular vesicles (EVs). This review examines the biological features, analytical technologies, and clinical applications of these analytes in BC, with particular attention to two rapidly evolving areas. First, we discuss how artificial intelligence and machine learning are being applied to multi-analyte liquid biopsy data, from methylation- and fragmentomics-based classifiers for early detection to models integrating ctDNA and CTC information for resistance profiling and treatment-response prediction, while critically examining current limits in clinical validation and interpretability. Second, we address the role of serial ctDNA monitoring in the neoadjuvant setting, where it can refine risk stratification beyond pathologic complete response and identify candidates for early therapeutic escalation, reflected in intervention trials now testing this approach prospectively. We also cover established roles of these analytes in treatment monitoring, minimal residual disease (MRD) detection, resistance tracking, and metastatic disease management, alongside persistent barriers to routine adoption, including limited early-stage ctDNA shedding, clonal hematopoiesis, and inconsistent analytical standardization. As these technologies mature, liquid biopsy is poised to move from a prognostic tool toward one that guides personalized treatment in BC. Not applicable. This article is a narrative review. Liquid biopsy enables longitudinal profiling of breast cancer biology. ctDNA, CTCs, and EVs provide complementary biological information. ctDNA detection can precede breast cancer relapse by approximately 10–12 months. PADA-1 showed improved PFS with plasma-guided ESR1-directed switching. Multi-analyte approaches may improve prediction beyond single biomarkers.

items.title: LLM time machines: Valuing digital goods over time
items.abstract: Digital goods generate substantial consumer welfare, but their valuations are difficult to estimate because many are free to consumers. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can reconstruct these valuations over time using incentive-compatible binary choice experiments. We benchmark predictions against eight waves of representative US survey data collected between 2016 and 2024. Calibrating GPT-4-Turbo on one year, we find that it approximates the magnitude and temporal patterns of median human valuations in other years. Newer models do not necessarily improve predictions, tending to favor monetary compensation. Our findings suggest opportunities and limitations for longitudinal valuations using LLMs.

items.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
items.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

items.title: Making programming learning visible: Students’ perceptions of an authentic, process-oriented assessment design
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has increased questions about whether a final code artefact alone can constitute sufficient evidence of student learning in programming education. This poster presents a practice-based evaluation of a redesigned second-year programming unit that incorporated multiple forms of evidence of learning. The assessment design is informed by authentic assessment (Boud & Molloy, 2013), feedback for learning (Carless & Boud, 2018) and self-explanation theory (Chi et al., 1989). It responded to current calls for assessment reform in the age of AI by shifting attention from the final artefact to the processes through which students design, explain, test and improve code (Lodge et al., 2023). Across three progressively sequenced assessments, students produced working Python programs, submitted WakaTime development records, recorded video explanations of design decisions, declared and justified GenAI use where permitted, and revisited prior code to improve exception handling and pytest testing. GenAI was allowed under accountable-use conditions, during which students were required to identify GenAI-assisted code, ensure that their submissions used concepts taught in the unit, and demonstrate that they understood and could explain the code they submitted. Assessment 1 established foundational object-oriented programming practices. Assessment 2 asked students to build a weather-data bot using CSV data, web scraping, datetime, logging, collections and pandas analysis. Assessment 3 required students to return to their Assessment 2 codebase and use feedback from Assessment 2 to strengthen its robustness through built-in exceptions, custom exceptions and tests. The design operationalised process-oriented assessment at task level. Code provided product evidence; WakaTime provided process evidence; video explanation provided conceptual evidence; and feedback with staged task design supported iterative development. Together, these tasks created an evidentiary architecture that made programming processes, conceptual reasoning and judgement more visible than final code alone. The evaluation drew on 68 anonymous unit feedback responses. Open-ended feedback was examined using thematic analysis (Clarke & Braun, 2017). Three student-perception themes were emergent. First, authentic tasks positioned programming as professional practice: students valued project-based tasks such as CSV analysis, web scraping and data-processing bots because they resembled meaningful programming work. Second, explanation and process evidence made computational thinking visible: students described shifts from writing code to thinking in terms of modularity, validation, debugging and engineering practice. Third, feedback supported iterative improvement and confidence: students reported that feedback helped them identify errors, revise code and progress more independently. The poster argues that process-oriented programming assessment should not rely only on restricting AI use. Instead, assessment can require multiple forms of evidence to validate student learning (Dawson et al., 2024) such as working code, development traces, self-explanatory video, feedback uptake, accountable AI-use declarations and testing artefacts. Video explanation is especially important because it prompts students to justify programing structures, methods, strategies and data-analysis approaches (Lai & Niblock, 2024). The study is limited by its reliance on one unit, one teaching period and self-reported student feedback. Further analysis of WakaTime data, video explanations, code revisions and pytest artefacts will examine how process evidence relates to conceptual understanding, reasoning and feedback uptake.

items.title: Management Communication in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: Reframing Human Connection, Trust and Leadership Voice in the Algorithmic Workplace
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now drafts memos, summarises meetings, translates messages, analyses employee sentiment and answers customers, placing it at the centre of how managers communicate. This paper examines how these developments are reshaping management communication and what they demand of managers. Using a documented integrative review of 49 sources from management, organisational communication and human–computer interaction, it integrates media richness, sensemaking, sociotechnical systems and organisational trust theories into a multi-level account. A consolidated evidence table and a comparative analysis of seven AI applications show that AI improves the speed, clarity and reach of routine, informational communication, but that messages perceived as heavily AI-written lower judgements of the sender's sincerity, authenticity and trustworthiness, especially for relational and high-stakes messages, and that disclosure alone does not remove this penalty. The paper argues that AI changes the mechanics of management communication more readily than its meaning. It examines the Nigerian context in depth, including infrastructure, linguistic diversity, high power distance and the 2025 data protection directive, together with implementation barriers at technological, organisational, individual, cultural and regulatory levels. It then proposes the Human-Centred AI Communication (HCAIC) framework and positions it against existing frameworks. HCAIC comprises six practices (strategic intent, human oversight, authenticity and transparency, ethical data governance, capability building and employee participation), which act through perceived authenticity, message accuracy and psychological safety to produce trust, clarity and employee voice. Key concepts are operationalised and seven propositions are offered for empirical testing. The paper concludes that the defining managerial competence of the AI era is not generating messages, but making messages mean something to people.

items.title: Management of Behavioral Addictions via Artificial Intelligence based Digital Technologies
items.abstract: Behavioral addictions, such as problematic gaming, gambling, social media use, and online shopping, have emerged as a growing global concern with significant psychological, social, and economic consequences. Traditional assessment and treatment approaches, while clinically grounded, often struggle with scalability, accessibility, and long-term engagement. In recent years, advances in digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled the development of novel, data-driven solutions for the prevention, detection, treatment, and recovery of behavioral addictions. This book presents a comprehensive survey of the management of behavioral addictions through digital technologies, bridging clinical foundations with state-of-the-art computational approaches. This book aims to provide researchers, clinicians, and practitioners with a unified, interdisciplinary perspective on the opportunities and limitations of AI-based digital technologies in behavioral addiction management,and to highlight pathways toward more scalable, personalized, and effective intervention strategies.

items.title: Managers-as-coaches in digitally mediated work: a practice-based framework for reflective leadership and workplace learning
items.abstract: Purpose This paper examines how reflective judgement is supported through audio-only coaching by managers in digitally mediated work and develops a practice-based framework for reflective leadership and workplace learning, with bounded implications for artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled learning. Design/methodology/approach Practitioner-led, work-applied action research was conducted in a global business-to-business (B2B) sales organisation. The research material comprised contemporaneous written records of fourteen audio-only coaching conversations, participant feedback and reflective journals, as well as approximately one hundred on-the-go records spanning more than one year. Reflexive thematic analysis followed an interpretivist orientation. Findings Four recurring micro-processes were identified: reflective attention, motivational nourishment, value-based reframing and metacognitive regulation. They were most visible when the manager restrained authority, protected silence and left interpretation and action with participants but weakened in urgent exchanges. Audio-only mediation appeared to support openness and listening when combined with relational familiarity, participant preference and protected time. Research limitations/implications The single-organisation design and reliance on contemporaneous written records constrain transferability claims and fine-grained interactional analysis; implications for AI-enabled coaching remain conceptual. Practical implications Managers can use the four micro-processes to preserve reflection and ownership; human resource development (HRD) practitioners can use the framework to design and evaluate digital coaching as workplace learning. Social implications Preserving employees' ownership of judgement may support responsible participation and attention to stakeholder consequences. Originality/value The study integrates four empirically grounded micro-processes into a practice-based framework for reflective workplace learning and offers a bounded, literature-informed bridge between managerial dependency and potential algorithmic conformity.

items.title: Mapping the Evolution of Digital Health Innovation Using an Agentic AI-Assisted Longitudinal Horizon-Scanning Methodology
items.abstract: Background: Increasing volumes of heterogeneous digital-health intelligence challenge conventional horizon-scanning methods and their ability to examine how technologies, clinical priorities and innovation pathways evolve over time. This study developed an agentic AI-assisted methodology for longitudinal digital-health horizon scanning. Methods: We analysed 123 NHS horizon scans conducted in 2015 and annually from 2019 to 2026, comprising 4,039 company-year profiles. Horizon-scan records were integrated with policy, clinical, funding and media evidence. Entity harmonisation, transformer-based semantic representations, TF-IDF analysis, machine learning and semantic clustering were used to characterise thematic evolution and estimate next-year corpus reappearance and future documented maturity. Performance was evaluated using nested company-grouped and rolling-origin validation, and candidate themes were contextualised through human-reviewed multi-agent synthesis. Results: The corpus shifted from enterprise, workforce and operational technologies towards condition-specific clinical applications, including oncology, women’s health, cardiovascular care, cognitive assessment, neurodevelopmental conditions and imaging artificial intelligence. Under nested company-grouped validation, XGBoost estimated next-year corpus reappearance with an F1 score of 0.67, ROC-AUC of 0.89 and average precision of 0.72. Extra Trees estimated future documented maturity with R2=0.40and RMSE =0.96, compared with R2=0.27and RMSE =1.05for direct carry-forward. Chronological performance was more variable across annual cohorts. Conclusions: The framework provides a structured and traceable approach for transforming historical horizon scans into longitudinal thematic intelligence, company-level estimates and candidate areas for further investigation. It is intended to augment expert-led horizon scanning rather than replace clinical, regulatory, procurement or commissioning judgement.

items.title: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning
items.abstract: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by increased cumulative regret. To address this problem, we introduce Learned Pseudo-Count MCTS (LPC-MCTS), which changes only the exploration statistic in UCT. A lightweight Coin-Flipping Network head on the policy's hidden representations estimates representation coverage, enabling related branches to share exploration evidence. Across 5 mathematical-reasoning and 7 search benchmarks, LPC-MCTS consistently outperforms strong MCTS baselines. Holding each LPC-MCTS-trained policy fixed, replacing standard MCTS counts at inference improves average mean@16 accuracy across 5 mathematical benchmarks by 3.79 percentage points on Qwen2.5-7B and 2.71 points on Qwen3-4B. Applying LPC-MCTS during both training and inference yields gains of 4.96 and 4.37 points over standard MCTS, respectively. Together, our theory and experiments show that changing what MCTS counts can substantially improve its exploration efficiency and reasoning performance.

items.title: Meaningful work in a male-dominated profession: a thematic analysis of women Neapolitan pizza chefs
items.abstract: Purpose This research examined how women pizza chefs construct, negotiate and experience meaningful work within the traditionally male-dominated context of the Neapolitan pizza sector. Design/methodology/approach This study adopted a qualitative research design. Data were collected through 25 semi-structured interviews and analysed using thematic analysis to identify recurring themes and patterns. Findings The findings reveal three interconnected processes through which meaningful work is constructed and negotiated: legitimacy construction, resistance to gender norms and identity transformation. Meaningfulness emerges through ongoing efforts to gain professional recognition, challenge gendered expectations and redefine professional identities within a male-dominated and culturally embedded occupation. Relational dynamics, including customer recognition, mentoring and family support, act as enabling conditions that sustain these processes over time. Originality/value This study highlights how women negotiate their professional identities and define what makes their work meaningful in artisanal and culturally embedded occupations while navigating gendered barriers in hospitality and restaurant contexts.

items.title: Measuring and Mitigating Forgetting when Extending a PDE Foundation Model to Simulated Flow Regimes
items.abstract: Foundation models for partial differential equations adapt efficiently to new tasks, but their effect on the original pretraining distribution is rarely measured. We study this retention problem on Poseidon, a neural operator pretrained on periodicdomain compressible Euler and incompressible Navier–Stokes families. We adapt it to two regimes absent from pretraining, a compressible Kelvin–Helmholtz flow and wall-bounded flow past a circular cylinder. Fine-tuning adapts efficiently but degrades the pretraining families. LoRA still forgets substantially, and freezing the whole trunk reduces forgetting without preventing it. We show that low-weight replay and joint training resolve this trade-off, extending the model to the new regimes while keeping the pretraining families near their original accuracy. These results suggest that lightweight replay can extend a PDE foundation model while substantially preserving its existing capabilities.

items.abstract: Marbleslides as an effective tool for forming the mathematical and ICT competences of primary school students. The author examines the problem of overcoming cognitive barriers in studying the topic "Quadratic Function" in the 9th grade, which arise due to the high level of abstraction of educational material and the static nature of traditional visualization tools. The relevance of the study is driven by the need to modernize the educational process in the context of implementing the "New Ukrainian School" concept, which requires a shift from reproductive learning to active research activity and mathematical modeling. Within the framework of the study, the methodology for organizing students’ independent search activities in a specially created creative learning environment is detailed. Particular attention is paid to the transformation of a learning error from a stress factor into an effective diagnostic tool through the mechanism of instantaneous visual and kinetic feedback provided by the Marbleslides simulation. The paper describes a step-by-step process of a student’s transition from empirical guessing of parabola parameters to conscious mathematical design and verification of hypotheses based on the analysis of dynamic changes in the graph. The didactic stages of working with the simulation are analyzed: from "visual provocation" and experimental search for the role of coefficient a and constant term c to the final synthesis of knowledge and the formation of stable cognitive connections between the analytical notation of a function and its geometric image. It is proved that the integration of Marbleslides into the educational process allows for the implementation of an exploratory approach, where the solution of standard problems is transformed into intellectual modeling of dynamic processes. It is determined that such an approach not only contributes to a deep understanding of the properties of a quadratic function, but also stimulates the development of functional thinking, increases cognitive activity and intrinsic motivation of ninth-graders to study algebra. The results of the study can be used by mathematics teachers to design original learning activities and modernize the educational process.

items.title: Mind the Gap: A Deployed Multi-Agent System for Documentation Maintenance
items.abstract: The "AI revolution" has enabled teams across the technology industry to deliver software features at unprecedented velocity. While code evolves faster than ever, customer-facing documentation often struggles to stay up to speed. As users increasingly rely on LLM-based agents that consume documentation as their primary interface, the impact of this documentation gap worsens: stale information propagates and is treated as authoritative. Signals for identifying where documentation has fallen behind already exist in abundance, both explicit (e.g., resolved support tickets revealing what documentation lacks) and implicit (e.g., code-documentation discrepancies detectable from automated loops). We deploy a multi-agent system, built around a triage agent we call "TriAgent," that continuously extracts these signals and repairs documentation drift. Over 43 days of shadow-mode operation, our system triaged 499 tickets and surfaced 92 gaps in the documentation. Using a panel of LLM judges from independent model families, 81.1% of TriAgent's verifiable assertions were correct (245 of the 302 assertions the human resolution addresses; majority of three judges); on length-comparable pairs the panel preferred TriAgent's response in 70.5% of pairs and the human engineer's in 23.2% (the rest had no judge majority). items.title: Mind the gap: Bridging disconnection in Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL) design
items.abstract: As higher education continues to rapidly digitise with the rise of Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL), the challenge is not only technology implementation or access, but meaningful integration into student-facing learning, assessment, communication and support practices (Chung et al., 2026). Despite increasing investment in TEL, research and practice continues to focus on technology adoption, functionality and efficiency (Feng et al., 2025; Wu & Chen, 2025). Consequently, learning technologies, pedagogy and student services are often treated as separate domains rather than interconnected components of an educational ecosystem (Barrett & Harte, 2023; Børte & Lillejord, 2024). This creates a design problem where students experience fragmentation across systems, processes and support services, leading to disconnection between learning and assessment. Drawing on practice-based evidence and relevant literature, this poster argues that advancing TEL requires intentionally designing connection across the educational ecosystem. This poster employs a practice-based, reflective methodology informed by evidence gathered across two intersecting roles at a research-intensive metropolitan university in Australia. First, as an educational developer involved in learning design, digital assessment implementation, and academic capability development. Second, as a strategic student experience officer within a stakeholder relations team, focused on cross-functional collaboration, service design, stakeholder engagement, and student support. Insights were drawn from implementation observations on digital assessment initiatives, stakeholder interactions across faculties and central service divisions, service-design challenges and student support queries. Recent literature on digital transformation, TEL, student wellbeing, and connected learning ecosystems was used to sensitise and critically inform these reflections, providing a conceptual lens through which patterns and gaps could be identified. This contributed to the development of a conceptual framework that positions learning, support, and technology as interconnected components of a connected educational ecosystem. Insights from the roles highlighted recurring points of disconnection in student facing practices, including assessment processes, support pathways and learning design decisions. These issues emerged at the intersections between academic, professional and technological domains, and were often reinforced by siloed approaches to working. These practice-informed reflections suggest that the future of digital learning depends on the intentional design of connection across students, educators, professional staff, and institutional systems. When learning, assessment, and support are designed in isolation, misalignment and fragmentation can occur, with implications for student success, satisfaction, and motivation (Bull, 2025; Liang et al., 2024). The implications on TEL are to prioritise collaborative connections across student-facing practices. To address the disconnect gap, the poster proposes a “Connection by Design” framework, developed through an iterative process of reflective analysis, stakeholder consultation, and engagement with literature on TEL, student wellbeing, digital transformation and connected learning. Practice-based observations from digital assessment implementation, service design initiatives, stakeholder interactions, support queries, and communication challenges were compared against themes from relevant literature and refined through ongoing professional dialogue, peer feedback, and cross-functional collaboration. This process contributed to the identification of three interdependent dimensions of effective TEL design. The first is human connection, which focuses designing learning and assessment that promote clarity, belonging and productive cognitive engagement (Zhou & Ye, 2024). The second is collaborative connection, which highlights the importance of co-design between academics, education designers and technologists and professional staff. The third is systemic connection, which involves the alignment of digital platforms and services through integration, policy coherence and embedded support pathways. Together, these three dimensions provide a practical approach for diagnosing disconnection and informing more connected, collaborative and human-centred TEL design.

items.title: Miscalibrated AI improves human calibration: An alignment problem for AI-assisted Decision education
items.abstract: Using artificial intelligence (AI) well requires probabilistic thinking, and central to it is calibration: expressing certainty that matches one's actual accuracy. Calibration is a decision skill, but a notoriously difficult one to teach. Because AI systems typically generate a probability alongside every prediction, observing these probabilities may help humans learn to provide better calibrated judgments. This is one form of what we call AI-assisted decision education -- using AI to teach the judgment skills that decision-making requires -- of which learning by observation, as here, is among the simplest forms. In a preregistered experiment, novice participants (N = 300) judged the probability that images of white blood cells were cancerous, before and after exposure to a highly accurate (94%) convolutional neural network. A single model was shown in three ways, holding accuracy fixed while varying the certainty it expressed: its original probabilities, which were conservative and poorly calibrated for the model's accuracy; a recalibrated version, well calibrated for the model and correspondingly certain; or categorical predictions carrying no probability information. When later tested without the AI, only the original, conservative display improved participants' calibration. It did so by reducing over-extremity, without a condition-specific improvement in discrimination. Notably, the display that taught best was the one miscalibrated for the model. AI-assisted decision education therefore faces an alignment problem: the signal that best describes a model, need not be the signal that best supports the learner.

items.title: Mitigating the Negative Consequences of Work Stressors: The Role of Perceived Meaning and Calling
items.abstract: The purpose of the present study was to understand how meaningful work and vocational calling may benefit employees’ work and well-being under circumstances of job stressors. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources framework, we tested a model linking stressor exposure to work and health outcomes through one’s experience of meaningful work, and dependent on one’s perception of work calling via a two time-point survey of 493 employees. Exposure to particular stressors and evaluated workplace and health-relevant outcomes were consistently linked, and further support was found for the role of calling in buffering the impact of certain stressors on outcomes through work meaning. This study contributes to the occupational health and career development literatures by expanding our understanding of detriments to job-related (i.e., job satisfaction and turnover intentions) and well-being-related (i.e., physical symptoms and burnout) criterion variables from workplace stressors. Implications for organizations and counselors, study limitations, and future directions are discussed.

items.title: More Than a Score: Reinforcement Learning with Verbalized Feedback for Generative Recommendation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for generative recommendation, where recommended items are generated directly from users' interaction histories. To further improve recommendation quality, reinforcement learning (RL) has been applied to align these models with recommendation objectives. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar rewards to implicitly guide exploration. These rewards do not specify which aspects of a candidate conflict with the user's preferences or how the next candidate should differ. To address this gap, we propose VerRec, a verbalized feedback-guided RL framework for generative recommendation. Specifically, a user simulator generates personalized verbalized feedback based on the user's historical preferences and the candidate item profile. The policy uses this feedback to produce refined recommendations. Original and refined candidates form an expanded group and are jointly optimized with group relative policy optimization. The user simulator is only required during training and is removed at inference time. Experiments on three Amazon review datasets with two generative recommendation backbones demonstrate that VerRec improves recommendation accuracy and ranking quality. Further analyses show that verbalized guidance encourages exploration of more diverse candidates and helps the policy discover more rewarding recommendations during training.

items.title: More than a Second Pair of Eyes: Artificial Intelligence Across the Breast Imaging Pathway
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from stand-alone accuracy studies to prospective deployment across breast screening, risk prediction, multimodal diagnosis, treatment response, and workflow support. The goal of this narrative review is to determine which AI applications have demonstrated clinical benefit, which remain technically promising, and what safeguards are required for implementation. We synthesize randomized trials, prospective cohorts, real-world implementations, external validations, systematic reviews, and guidance identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus through 30 June 2026. In screening, AI-supported mammography can increase cancer detection and reduce reading workload, but effects depend on whether AI is used as concurrent support, an independent reader, triage, or partial autonomy; autonomous workflows may shift work and cost downstream through additional recalls. MASAI met its prespecified noninferiority criterion for interval cancer, but this should not be interpreted as proof of equivalence or mortality benefit. Image-based risk models often discriminate better than density or conventional clinical models, although prospective benefit from AI-guided allocation to supplemental imaging has not yet been demonstrated. Evidence for contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM), MRI, ultrasound, radiomics, and multimodal models is less mature and limited by external validation, domain shift, missing data, operator dependence, and uncertain incremental value beyond clinicopathological factors. Ungrounded large language models and opaque foundation models are not suitable for autonomous clinical advice. Current evidence therefore supports controlled, task-specific integration rather than radiologist replacement; real clinical benefit depends on governance of the whole AI-enabled pathway, including local validation, human factors, downstream resource use, statistical stopping rules, and fallback procedures.

items.title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
items.abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

items.title: Multi-View Synergistic Learning with Vision-Language Adaptation for Low-Resource Biomedical Image Classification
items.abstract: Accurate biomedical image classification under limited supervision remains challenging due to scarce annotations, subtle inter-class differences, and complex disease semantics. Pretrained vision-language models offer a promising foundation for alleviating data scarcity through knowledge transfer, yet effectively adapting them to low-resource biomedical tasks remains nontrivial. To this end, we propose Multi-View Synergistic Learning (MVSL), a unified framework that jointly considers three complementary perspectives: adaptation paradigms, representation granularity, and disease semantic relationships. Specifically, MVSL adopts tailored adaptation strategies for visual and textual encoders, accommodating their distinct representational characteristics while preserving pretrained knowledge. To capture both holistic image semantics and localized pathological evidence, we introduce multi-granularity contrastive learning that aligns global image representations and local visual features with disease-specific textual embeddings. Furthermore, we develop a Disease Semantic Graph (DSG) that leverages disease descriptions generated by large language models to model class-level semantic relationships and regularize adapted textual representations, thereby complementing discriminative learning and helping mitigate excessive specialization toward observed categories. Through the synergy of these complementary perspectives, MVSL enhances fine-grained discrimination while supporting semantic consistency and generalization to unseen categories. Extensive experiments on 11 public biomedical datasets spanning 9 imaging modalities and 10 anatomical regions demonstrate the effectiveness of MVSL in few-shot classification and base-to-novel generalization. The implementation and detailed experimental results are publicly available at https://github.com/luoxiaoliu/MVSL.

items.title: Multidimensional ageing reserve and 10-year all-cause mortality among older adults in China: a prospective cohort study of the Chinese longitudinal healthy longevity survey
items.abstract: Background Dietary, behavioral, psychological, and engagement resources may jointly be associated with survival in later life. We examined the association between a multidimensional ageing reserve (MDAR) index and all-cause mortality among older Chinese adults. Methods The 2008–2009 baseline data from the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS) were linked to subsequent mortality records. MDAR combined four equally weighted standardized domains: dietary diversity, lifestyle behavior, psychosocial wellbeing, and activity/social-cognitive engagement. Follow-up was censored at 10 years. Cox models compared MDAR quartiles and estimated a linear summary association per standard deviation (SD). Restricted cubic splines assessed non-linearity. Complete-case analyses were supplemented by multiple imputation, a 2-year landmark analysis, attained-age models, and weighted analyses. Results Among the 10,249 participants (mean age 85.2 years; 53.7% women), 6,569 deaths occurred over 51,534 person-years. Fully adjusted hazard ratios (HRs; 95% confidence intervals [CIs]) relative to the lowest quartile were 0.94 (0.88–1.01), 0.99 (0.92–1.06), and 0.85 (0.78–0.93) for quartiles 2, 3, and 4, respectively. The linear summary hazard ratio per SD was 0.93 (0.90–0.96). The spline indicated non-linearity ( p = 0.007), with a more pronounced inverse association at higher scores. items.title: Multimodal Physiological and EEG Responses to Short‐Term Hypobaric Hypoxia Exposure: Evidence of Central–Peripheral Coordination
items.abstract: Low‐pressure environments are common in aircraft cabins and high‐altitude operations, where reduced oxygen partial pressure alters human physiological regulation, energy metabolism, and cognitive performance. However, existing studies primarily focus on isolated physiological responses, lacking a systematic understanding of the coupling between central neural activity and peripheral physiological adaptation under short‐term hypobaric hypoxia exposure. In this study, a controlled experiment was conducted in a hypobaric chamber under three pressure conditions (101.3, 67.2, and 56.1 kPa). Multimodal data, including electroencephalography (EEG), heart rate (HR), blood oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ), and respiratory‐metabolic parameters, were synchronously collected to characterize human responses across pressure levels and exposure time. Results showed that decreasing pressure significantly increased metabolic demand, with HR rising by 3.7%–5.8%, SpO 2 decreasing from 98.2% to 86.5%, and respiratory rate and metabolic rate markedly elevated, indicating typical hypoxic compensation. At the neural level, EEG spectral power shifted from low‐frequency (δ and θ) to high‐frequency (α and β) bands, with enhanced activity in frontal and occipital regions, suggesting increased cognitive resource allocation. Significant correlations between EEG features and peripheral physiological indices further revealed a coordinated central–peripheral coupling mechanism. This study provides a novel integrative perspective linking environmental pressure, metabolic cost, and neural regulation, offering new insights for cabin pressure design, human performance assessment, and human–environment interaction modeling in built environments.

items.title: Navigating curricular complexity: Programmatic assessment and AI in a business context
items.abstract: Traditional models of programmatic assessment are historically rooted in highly structured, linear disciplines such as medicine (Heeneman et al., 2015; Torre et al., 2021). Translating these principles to a diverse, modular Business and Economics faculty presents profound curricular, structural, and governance challenges. Business courses within Monash University operate within a flexible architecture designed to support highly personalized student pathways, where over 90% of students have unique pathways via diverse combinations of majors, minors, and electives. Consequently, units are highly interconnected—sometimes contributing to up to 20 distinct programs—so that an assessment alteration in one unit ripples across multiple independent degree structures. This structural friction is compounded by distributed governance split across separate academic departments, departmental Directors of Education (DOEs), Course Directors, and Chief Examiners. To navigate this complex landscape, the Senior Educational Designer and the Associate Dean of Learning and Teaching (ADLT) collaborated on a university-wide initiative entitled Programmatic Assessment and Artificial Intelligence Review (PAAIR) spurred by TEQSA requirements (Lodge et al., 2023). We adapted established theory around programmatic assessment to synthesize a tailored five-principle framework, designating “Collaborative and Transparent Culture” as Principle 1. To address modular friction, we drew on Dawson’s (2020) concept of programmatic assessment security, shifting the unit of analysis from hardening every individual, isolated module to strategically securing key programmatic assessment moments across the entire course. Cultivating this shared-accountability mindset was critical because curriculum reviews occurred by course, where a single unit could feed into multiple programs with diverse departmental oversight. It was difficult to have a unified, static “full picture” of a complete course at any one stage of a review, as some units may have been completed as part of other reviews, or they may be dual-coded with a postgraduate course, requiring complex cross-referencing across courses, departments, year levels, and campuses. To bridge this diagnostic gap, we collaborated with the faculty’s data analytics team to develop the PAAIR Dashboard in PowerBI. Serving as an interactive visual analytics platform, the dashboard empowers DOEs, Course Leaders, and Educational Designers to see beyond disciplinary silos, map competency coverage across shared pathways, monitor assessment distributions, and facilitate data-informed co-design conversations in real time. It helps flag structural gaps—such as when a core graduate competency is not assessed under secure conditions at least twice per year level—ensuring curriculum resilience across highly complex student pathways. At the launch of the project, we developed a comprehensive suite of guidelines to support Unit Learning Outcome (ULO) refinement, Course Learning Outcome (CLO) mapping, and balanced assessment design. These guidelines have been instrumental in improving our course designs by scaffolding competencies progressively and designing assessment tasks with and without generative AI (Lodge et al., 2023; Matheis & John, 2024). This dual approach balances the educative, values-driven framework of academic integrity with the adversarial, hardening requirements of assessment security (Dawson, 2020). As the initiative now enters the initial transition to Business-As-Usual (BAU) operations, we are actively developing a future governance strategy to manage subsequent curriculum changes sustainably. This Pecha Kucha presentation delivers a transparent roadmap and strategic recommendations for other modular higher education faculties seeking to operationalize programmatic assessment and AI review within highly complex, non-linear educational ecosystems.

items.title: Negotiating identity and relationality: An AI-enhanced polylogue on human-centred learning design practices
items.abstract: This poster presents a developing AI-enhanced polylogue methodology and conceptual framing to understand how third-space professionals in higher education are negotiating their shifting roles and identities while designing human-centred learning and assessment. Recent technological disruptions (e.g., widespread proliferation, advancement and use of generative AI, focus on cybersecurity, adoption of data-enabled technologies and ecosystems) have intensified tensions around higher education assessment structures and practices, exposing the limitations of isolated, task-based evaluation of student learning (Boud et al., 2020; Corbin et al., 2025). In response to the challenges posed to learning and assessment in the contemporary higher education landscape, emerging scholarship has foregrounded relationality and human connection alongside a shift to more program-wide approaches to assessment and assurance of learning (Lodge et al., 2023; Nicola-Richmond et al., 2025). This has highlighted questions about how educators can sustain meaningful relationships with each other and with students amidst these disruptions (Maldon et al., 2025). In this work-in-progress project, we focus on these relational questions and explore how technological disruptions are reshaping the roles and identities of educators, specifically curriculum designers working in third-space roles at the boundary of academic and professional domains (Whitchurch, 2012). We build on work that positions teaching and learning as fundamentally relational, emphasising connection, trust, care, and dialogue between educators, students, and third-space professionals (Riddle & Hickey, 2023). Our aim is to understand how relationality may be conceptualised in the context of transforming curriculum to support human flourishing and critical engagement with generative AI in our everyday learning design practice, particularly in the design of program-level assessment, feedback, mentorship, and collaborative sense-making structures. The project employs an AI-enhanced polylogue methodology inspired by Markauskaite et al. (2022). The AI-enhanced polylogue is a structured, multi-voiced inquiry, where participants engage in iterative cycles of individual reflection and collaborative dialogue, involving AI as a reflective interlocutor to surface gaps, alternative perspectives, and assumptions. Over several months, three curriculum designers independently responded to targeted questions in reflective logbooks, then engaged in semi-structured conversations about connection in higher education, program-level learning design, evolving educator roles, and the contributions of third-space professionals. This was complemented by a collaborative chat with a generative AI tool, in which participants used AI to probe gaps, tensions, and alternative perspectives arising from the conversations. These strands are then brought together in collaborative critical reflection sessions to identify emerging patterns in relational practice and their significance in program-level curriculum design. This poster shares early themes from the logbooks and conversations. Early analysis highlights how participants experience and navigate tensions between increasing technological mediation alongside their third-space roles and their commitment to relational practice. The importance of human-centred learning design and its implications will also be examined and shared. The project contributes to contemporary discussions on inter-collegial practices that keep connection, trust, and dialogue central in increasingly AI-mediated educational environments. As part of this project, participants treat disruption as an invitation to remake educator identities and practices in more relational, collaborative, and inclusive ways.

items.title: Network-Exposed Configuration Attacks on LLM-Controlled Social Robots
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in embodied robots create security dependencies beyond inference. We investigate a network-exposed configuration attack on the Pollen Robotics Reachy Mini Lite, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to replace personality settings and the cloud LLM's system prompt through a management interface, without adversarial conversational input. Eleven prompt-injection attempts across five categories were reported as resisted, whereas both configuration-layer attack paths produced observable behavioural changes on physical hardware. We demonstrate local and network-adjacent access, mapping the weakness to CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for a Critical Function) and CWE-1327 (Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address), with a reported CVSS v3.1 score of 6.5 (Medium). A configuration endpoint also accepts cross-origin requests without a CORS preflight (CWE-352; 6.5 Medium), while the persistent-memory sink stores content without enforcing its stated restrictions. A source review of 59 public repositories identifies missing authentication in 10 of 11 source-verifiable genuine applications, or 11 of 11 including a framework-default case. These findings indicate recurrence within the sampled repositories, not prevalence in commercial products. We characterise a deployment gap between developer-oriented network assumptions and consumer-facing embodied AI security: inference-layer refusal cannot prevent unauthorised changes to model instructions. Potential consequences include surveillance through onboard cameras and microphones and social engineering of nearby users. Proof-of-concept code, evidence and the survey are available at https://bit.ly/reachypi.

items.title: Neural tracking of phonological, lexical, and syntactic surprisal during naturalistic listening in elementary-aged children with and without dyslexia
items.abstract: Children with dyslexia show persistent phonological difficulties in controlled experiments yet often comprehend everyday spoken language successfully. The present study examined how children with and without dyslexia neurally track phonological, lexical, and syntactic information during naturalistic story listening, and how this tracking relates to reading proficiency. Children listened to a story during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Study 1 examined neural tracking in 140 typically developing (TD) children. Study 2 compared children with dyslexia with age- and gender-matched TD controls (n = 35 per group). Large language model-derived surprisal estimates indexed tracking at each level at exploratory and multiple comparison corrected thresholds. In TD children, each level of surprisal tracking showed a distinct cortical profile, and higher reading comprehension was associated with greater phonological and syntactic tracking, but reduced lexical tracking. Children with dyslexia also showed distinct tracking profiles across levels. In this group, however, higher reading proficiency was associated with greater lexical and syntactic tracking and reduced phonological tracking. Group contrasts mirrored these patterns. Children with and without dyslexia differ in how neural tracking of linguistic information relates to reading. In dyslexia, reduced phonological tracking alongside greater lexical tracking may reflect increased reliance on higher-level linguistic information. Syntactic tracking was positively related to reading proficiency in both groups, consistent with the protracted development of syntax and its contribution to literacy. These findings offer new insights into the real-time neurobiology of naturalistic language comprehension and how the interaction of underlying skills may vary in children with dyslexia.

items.title: Next-generation high performance MXene–MgF2 based wideband solar absorber with artificial intelligent optimization for renewable energy mining applications
items.abstract: Solar energy provides a promising and easily accessible renewable energy source when it comes to solving energy issues. Industries consume high amounts of energy for various uses. Thus, the concept of a solar absorber that absorbs wideband radiation is shown in this study. The absorber's configuration is MXene-Magnesium Fluoride-MXene. These structures create a novel geometry that traps the heat and absorbs a high amount of radiation. The proposed absorber's resonator layer geometry has a T-shape with a Nanodisk MXene-based resonator Solar Absorber, whose structure makes it polarization-insensitive. An average of 95.57% absorption was achieved within the range of 200-3000 nm, keeping absorptance above 96% over a bandwidth nm while exceeding 92% over a much wider bandwidth of around 2120 nm across the spectral spectrum under investigation. Moreover, this suggested absorber achieved 94.9% average absorption under AM 1.5. Examined several solar absorber structures and the findings. Optimized the design over several parameters and examined the outcome. Then, analyzed the Transverse Electric and magnetic fields with magnetic and electric colour-changing fields, which are described in the results section. The research presents clear engineering outcomes for solar thermal absorber design, with machine learning methods demonstrating the application of artificial intelligence in the study. The examination shows that the Machine Learning model's maximum achievable R 2 value of 0.93 for parameter change intends to minimize the simulation period by a quarter when compared with older methods, while minimizing other simulation needs. The high absorption rate with a unique resonator design is promising for applications as a renewable solar dryer for mining.

items.title: Nobody writes for the reader: Reading level in paediatric health guidance, real health queries and AI chatbot responses
items.abstract: Purpose To compare the reading level of paediatric health guidance, parents' own questions and artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot responses to those questions, and to test whether chatbots adapt to the reading level of the person asking. Methods Cross-sectional study, reported following the Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool (CHART), of 18,392 guideline pages (17,516 family-facing, 876 clinician-facing) from 86 organisations, 1,000 parent-authored questions sampled from 23,477 public forum posts, and 5,000 responses to those questions from five commercially deployed chatbots. Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL) was the primary outcome, with six secondary metrics. In a sub-study, 100 questions were resubmitted with an instruction to match the reader's level or to answer at sixth-grade level (1,500 responses). Results Median FKGL was 12.51 for clinician-facing guidance, 9.08 for family-facing guidance, 8.37 for chatbot responses and 6.15 for parents' questions. The American Medical Association sixth-grade standard was exceeded by 99.3% of clinician-facing pages, 92.6% of family-facing pages and 89.2% of chatbot responses. Every chatbot answered above the reading level of the question asked (median difference + 1.21 to + 3.57 grades). Given an explicit sixth-grade instruction, the median gap narrowed in every model and three of five answered below the reader's level. Conclusion Paediatric health information from institutions and chatbots alike is written above the level of its readers. Chatbots do not adapt to the reader by default, but can when instructed.

items.title: Nonlinear function regression using quantum ensemble learning
items.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and quantum technologies have driven the emergence of quantum machine learning, yet imperfections in near-term quantum devices remain a major obstacle for achieving practical quantum advantage. In the absence of fault-tolerant machines, ensemble learning, which combines multiple imperfect quantum devices, may unlock new quantum computing applications. Here, we introduce two ensemble-learning algorithms, namely Bagging and AdaBoost, for enhancing the accuracy of nonlinear regression problems. While Bagging trains variational quantum regressors independently, AdaBoost employs a sequential training strategy and achieves significantly better prediction accuracy. By incorporating systematic feature selection into our ensemble learning algorithms, we enhance their predictive power for highly nonlinear functions. We further improve prediction accuracy through a feature-to-qubit mapping strategy based on repeated feature encoding. The performance of our ensemble-based algorithms improves with both the number of regressors in the ensemble and the size of each regressor. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using four benchmarking functions with varying degrees of nonlinearity by relying on a feature pool limited to first- and second-order polynomial terms.

items.title: NVIDIA Kumo Tabular: Pushing the Accuracy-Efficiency Frontier for Tabular Prediction
items.abstract: We introduce Kumo Tabular, a family of open tabular foundation models for classification and regression, in three sizes: Kumo Tabular-S (27M parameters), Kumo Tabular-M (61M), and Kumo Tabular-L (214M). Pretrained only on artificial tables from the Kumo prior, they can make predictions on new tables without any training. In our approach, a table encoder compresses each row into an embedding, and an in-context learning transformer predicts the unlabeled rows from the labeled ones. Kumo Tabular introduces architectural innovations that improve both training stability and predictive performance, enabling the model to scale up to 150M cells on modern GPUs. Kumo Tabular-L ranks first on eight benchmarks: TabArena, TALENT, BeyondArena, ScoringBench, STRABLE, MulTaBench, RamanBench, and TabBench-Bio. These cover probabilistic regression, tables with over 1M rows or 100K columns, and tables with strings, text, or images. Accuracy improves with model size in all tested comparisons. All three sizes lie on the accuracy-speed frontiers of TabArena and BeyondArena. Kumo Tabular-L predicts faster than the runners-up, LimiX-2 on TabArena (36 times) and TabPFN-3.5 on BeyondArena (1.7 times). Weights and pretraining code are released under OpenMDW-1.1 and Apache 2.0, respectively.

items.title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
items.abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce OAK-Mind, a zerO-training, multi-Agent, Knowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

items.title: Occupational health-oriented reinforcement learning models for intelligent adjustment of college students’ employment stress
items.abstract: The stress of work is a significant issue in the occupational health arena for college students because of the uncertainty of employment, evolving labor market expectations and preparation for the world of work. The existing methods are mainly based on psychological assessment instead of intelligent adjustment of stress according to the occupational health. This study is to design an Adaptive Vortex Optimizer (AVO) based Attention-Based Dueling Deep Q-Network (AD-DQN) model for intelligent adjustment of college students'' employment stress based on personalized decision optimization. The Occupational Employment Stress dataset consists of 15,000 student responses from multiple data sources, including university career guidance, health questionnaires, academic profiles, internship experiences, and students'' self-reported stress responses. Imputation using the K-Nearest Neighbor, Min–Max normalization and outlier refinement are used to enhance data quality. Deep Autoencoder-based feature extraction aims to obtain compact representation by capturing salient occupational, behavioral and educational traits and removing redundant information. The proposed model is designed to use extracted features to optimize the learning parameters and exploration strategies using AVO for efficient convergence. An Attention Mechanism (AM) selects important occupational health and employment related stress signals whereas a Dueling DQN is used to construct an intervention policy for an individual by estimating state value and action advantage. Feedback is offered and the RL constantly adjusts recommendations, thereby furthering career readiness and stress regulation. Experiments conducted in Python show superior performance in terms of 0.982 Accuracy, 0.963 Recall, 0.97 AUC, 0.94 F1-Score and 0.91 Kappa when compared to existing models. From these results, the classification reliability and discriminative ability have been improved, balanced prediction performance and consistent decision making have been achieved. AVO-AD-DQN can support university career-counseling services by enabling personalized employment-stress assessment and adaptive stress-management recommendations.
